summary: New Hampshire Fish and Game, through Director Bernard W. Corson, expressed conditional support for ORV regulation, noting that the Interior Department's guidance is being used as a model for potential state legislation. The agency favored a permissive default approach—leaving lands open to ORVs unless there is a specific reason to restrict them—rather than blanket closures, with restrictions applied only when damage becomes evident from increased traffic. They believed this approach would improve the quality of the sport while protecting the land.

statement.text:
INTER-DEPARTMENT COMMUNICATION
DATE June 23, 1972
FROM
Bernard W. Corson
Director
AT (OFFICE) Fish and Game
Suprest Executive (
Executive Order 11644 -- The Use of Off-road Vehicles on Public Lands.
TO
Alexander M. Taft, Director Comprehensive Planning State House Concord, New Hampshire 03301
Dear Zandy:
Please be advised that the study committee appointed by the Governor under authority of H3 24, Chapter 49 is currently considering the problems associated with the use of ATV's or ORV's
As a guide for possible legislation, we are using the memorandum dated May 5, 1972, issued by the Department of Interior and Executive Order 11644. This is an excellent guide for promulgation of regulations by the Fish and Game Department on department owned land and water as well as those other State lands administered by DRED.
The committee referred to above will be considering, among other things, legislation to regulate private land use.
We would hope that designation of lands would follow the policy of leaving land open to ORY's until there is a reason for restricting them as opposed to a blanket restriction, and opening land where they are sure that no damage will result. In many areas, light use is not detrimental but if traffic becomes too heavy, then they can be restricted. This type of regulation improves the quality of the sport as long as utility remains at a lon level.
Sincerely yours,
51
-Bernard W. Corson Director
